New Zealand blue cod (Parapercis colias) reaches a maximum total length of 45 centimetres [Li = 45 centimetres], a size attained only by the largest individuals in exceptionally productive coastal populations. Field surveys conducted in the Marlborough Sounds indicate that females typically achieve a slightly smaller asymptotic size than males, although the difference is modest. This ultimate length is correlated with substantial body mass; the largest females can attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1.3 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 1.3 kilograms], representing the upper limit of somatic growth for the species. Growth rates are rapid during the first two years of life before decelerating markedly as individuals approach their maximum size, a pattern commonly observed in temperate reef fishes with determinate growth potential.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this protogynous hermaphrodite occurs at a total length of 14.5 centimetres [Lp = 14.5 centimetres], a threshold size that corresponds with a weight at puberty of 36.7 grams [Wwp = 36.7 grams]. This size-based transition is typical of many serranid fishes, where social structure and resource availability influence the timing of maturation. Individuals below this length are functionally immature, with undeveloped gonads and no evidence of spawning activity. The relationship between length and weight at maturity follows a power-law function derived from morphometric data, with the weight estimate reflecting the condition of an average fish at the pubertal length. Females may remain at this size for several months before undergoing the social and physiological changes associated with sex change in larger individuals.

Reproductive output is considerable during the spawning season, which peaks in austral spring. Females achieve a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 147,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 147,000 eggs per year] at the ambient water temperature of 12.6 °C [T = 12.6 °C]. This high fecundity is coupled with a spawning frequency that supports robust recruitment in unfished populations. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, settling onto rocky substrates where they remain until hatching, providing some protection from pelagic predators during the earliest developmental stages.

The early life history of this species begins with a small, fertilised ovum approximately 1.17 millimetres in diameter. Upon hatching, the lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva emerges with a wet weight at birth of 0.00084 grams [Wwb = 0.00084 grams], a minimal mass that necessitates rapid yolk absorption and the timely onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is brief, lasting only a few days before the mouth opens and the larva begins to capture small zooplankton. This critical transition to active feeding marks the point when mortality rates are highest, as newly hatched larvae must locate suitable prey in the pelagic environment while simultaneously avoiding predation from larger planktonic organisms. Survivorship through this period strongly influences subsequent year-class strength.

The maximum life span of New Zealand blue cod in the wild is approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 12.6 °C [T = 12.6 °C], as estimated from otolith-based age validation studies. This longevity is comparatively high for a temperate reef fish of its maximum size, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances moderate growth rates with extended reproductive opportunities. Older individuals, particularly large females prior to sex change, contribute disproportionately to annual egg production due to their elevated fecundity and experience-dependent spawning success. Populations subject to heavy fishing pressure often exhibit truncated age structures, with few individuals exceeding 8 to 10 years, which can reduce the reproductive resilience of the stock over time.
